title: The War on Poverty's Experiment in Public Medicine: Community Health Centers and the Mortality of Older Americans
research_question: Did the establishment of Community Health Centers, which delivered subsidized primary care to disadvantaged populations beginning in the mid-1960s, produce long-term improvements in health as measured by mortality rates? In particular, how did expanded access to primary care affect mortality among older adults, and through what channels (e.g., management of chronic conditions, prescription drug access, interactions with public health insurance) did any effects operate?
data_description: The authors compile newly digitized administrative records on the location and first-grant year of Community Health Centers (CHCs) from National Archives Community Action Program files, Federal Outlays files, and Public Health Service reports, identifying 117 counties receiving CHCs in fiscal years 1965–1974 and another 497 counties through 1980. These are linked to county-year mortality data from the 1959–1988 Vital Statistics Multiple-Cause of Death Files (universe of civilian deaths by cause, age, and county of residence), combined with population data (1960 Census, SEER) to construct age-adjusted, age-specific, and cause-specific mortality rates as well as infant mortality rates. Supplementary data include the 1963 and 1970 Survey of Health Services Utilization and Expenditures (utilization, regular source of care, prescription expenditures), the 1966–1968 Mortality Followback Survey, county-level Medicare expenditures and enrollment, American Hospital Association annual surveys (1948–1990), Regional Economic Information System transfers, and 1960 county characteristics from the Area Resource File.
institutional_context: In 1965, as part of the War on Poverty, the Office of Economic Opportunity (OEO) began funding Community Health Centers to deliver low-cost, comprehensive primary care, prescription medications, and auxiliary services (home visits, transportation, outreach) directly to poor and underserved communities, distinct from the contemporaneous insurance expansions of Medicare and Medicaid. CHCs charged on a sliding scale, located in disadvantaged neighborhoods, and operated in-house pharmacies. The program rolled out unevenly across U.S. counties between 1965 and 1974, reflecting what historians describe as a chaotic, idiosyncratic OEO grant-making process in which leading local advocates assembled proposals, rather than systematic targeting on health need. The 1975 Special Health Revenue Sharing Act later redirected funding toward rural medically underserved areas. By 1974, 117 counties had CHCs serving roughly 13,000 patients each annually, providing a staggered expansion of primary-care access against a backdrop of rapidly falling national mortality.

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.identification_strategy: DID — treatment = counties with CHCs, control = counties without CHCs; shock/instrument/cutoff = rollout of CHCs

key_variables.treatment: presence of a Community Health Center in a county
key_variables.control: counties without a Community Health Center

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: The introduction of Community Health Centers led to a significant reduction in mortality rates among older Americans.
